title: The March on Makkah
subtitle: Ten Thousand Believers, the Concession of Ramadan, and the Strategic Approach to Marr al-Zahran
summary: On the tenth day of Ramadan in the eighth year of the Hijrah, an army of ten thousand Muslim warriors set forth from Madinah toward Makkah—the largest force ever assembled under the banner of the Prophet. Moving across the rugged Hejaz under strict operational discipline, the Prophet granted a practical concession by breaking his fast at Kura' al-Ghamim to preserve his army's strength, safely positioning his forces at Marr al-Zahran on the very threshold of the sacred city.

sections.text: The Great Departure in the Month of Fasting

On Wednesday, the tenth of Ramadan in the eighth year after the Hijrah, the gates of Madinah opened to unleash the greatest expeditionary force assembled in Arabia since the dawn of the prophetic mission. Ten thousand devout warriors—comprising the Muhajirun, the Ansar, and allied bedouin tribes including Aslam, Ghifar, Muzaynah, Ashja', and Juhaynah—marched out under the unified black and white standards of Islam. The vast column was driven by a single transcendent purpose: the peaceful reclamation of the House of Allah from two centuries of idolatry.

The journey commenced during the intense heat of an Arabian summer while the entire army observed the Ramadan fast. Every step across the scorched desert dunes demanded supreme willpower and physical endurance. The disciplined vanguard proceeded southward via the ancient caravan highway, maintaining strict security protocols to prevent desert scouts from alerting the inhabitants of Makkah.
The Prophetic Concession at Kura' al-Ghamim

As the army traversed the rocky passes approaching Kura' al-Ghamim—a rugged desert valley located between Usfan and Makkah—the physical strain of continuous marching in full battle gear while fasting began to take a severe toll upon the men. Observing that fatigue was eroding the combat readiness of his companions, the Messenger of Allah ﷺ introduced a profound manifestation of practical mercy and legal flexibility.
In an authentic narration recorded in Sahih al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim, Abdullah ibn Abbas described this decisive moment:

خَرَجَ رَسُولُ اللَّهِ صلى الله عليه وسلم عَامَ الْفَتْحِ فِي رَمَضَانَ، فَصَامَ حَتَّى بَلَغَ الْكَدِيدَ ثُمَّ أَفْطَرَ، وَأَفْطَرَ النَّاسُ
'The Messenger of Allah ﷺ set out in the year of the Conquest during Ramadan; he fasted until he reached Al-Kadeed [near Kura' al-Ghamim], then he broke his fast, and the people broke their fast.' (Sahih al-Bukhari 4275; Sahih Muslim 1114)

To ensure that no soldier felt spiritual guilt for abandoning the fast during military necessity, the Prophet called for a vessel of water while seated high upon his camel. In full view of the entire army, he lifted the vessel and drank. When reports reached him that certain overzealous individuals continued to fast, he remarked: 'Those are the disobedient ones; those are the disobedient ones,' establishing that preserving the physical strength necessary for defending truth takes legal precedence over voluntary stringency.
The Joining of Allied Tribes and Family Reunion

As the great host progressed south through the settlements of Qudayd and Al-Juhfa, additional detachments from friendly desert tribes swelled their ranks. The powerful warriors of Banu Sulaym joined with a thousand armored cavalrymen under the leadership of Abbas ibn Mirdas, bringing the total strength of the army to over ten thousand seasoned fighters.

At Al-Juhfa, a dramatic and emotional encounter occurred. The Prophet's uncle, Al-Abbas ibn Abd al-Muttalib, rode into the camp accompanied by his family and household baggage. Having long maintained a discreet presence in Makkah monitoring developments, Al-Abbas was emigrating to Madinah to cast his lot permanently with the believers. The Prophet welcomed his uncle with immense warmth and relief, saying: 'You are the last of the Emigrants, just as I am the last of the Prophets.' Al-Abbas immediately joined the vanguard, providing invaluable strategic insight regarding the current political mood within Makkah.
Encampment at the Gates of the Sanctuary

By nightfall, after eight days of relentless desert travel, the vast army entered the broad fertile valley of Marr al-Zahran (modern-day Wadi Fatimah), situated a mere ten miles northwest of Makkah. Shielded by the steep basalt ridges encircling the valley, the Muslim forces pitched their camp in total silence, unnoticed by the unsuspecting citizens of the holy city.

The strategic brilliance of the march lay in its absolute surprise. By arriving on the direct threshold of Makkah without engaging in prior combat, the Prophet eliminated any possibility of a coordinated pagan defense, setting the stage for an unprecedented bloodless liberation that would alter the destiny of Arabia forever.
